title: Lamb or Mutton with Potatoes and Gravy

content.title: About
content.content: Lamb (or mutton) with potatoes and gravy is a classic dish that pairs tender sheep meat with soft potatoes covered in a flavorful sauce. The meat is rich in protein and iron, while the potatoes provide carbohydrates and potassium. The gravy, usually made from stock, cream or tomato base, adds moisture and depth of flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lamb has a distinct aroma compared to beef due to higher levels of certain fatty acids.
In many cultures, mutton is reserved for special occasions such as Easter or festivals.
Traditional preparation often involves slow braising in earthenware pots to retain juiciness.
Potatoes are frequently par‑fried until golden before being baked together with the meat.
Gravy may include herbs like rosemary, thyme, garlic, and paprika to enhance the taste.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Lamb provides complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support the immune system and hemoglobin formation.

items.title: Potatoes supply potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Lamb contains B12, B6, and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Gravy can add healthy fats
items.content: When made with olive oil or a modest amount of cream, the sauce provides beneficial fatty acids.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Lamb contains more saturated fat than some other meats; people with cardiovascular concerns should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to lamb proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol in creamy gravies
items.content: Gravies made with heavy cream can raise dietary cholesterol.

items.title: Risk of undercooking
items.content: Insufficiently cooked meat may harbor bacteria such as Salmonella or E. coli.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, typically as a portion of meat with potatoes drenched in gravy. It pairs well with vegetable salads, sauerkraut, or fresh bread. For a lighter version, use a low‑fat stock instead of cream in the sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 2 months. Reheat until the internal temperature reaches at least 74 °C (165 °F).
